extracted.intended_audience: entrepreneurs, manufacturers, business managers (early automobile industry and general manufacturing)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical principles for designing, manufacturing, pricing, selling, and servicing mass-market durable goods (illustrated by early automobile manufacture). Emphasizes prioritizing service and product design over finance, standardization with interchangeability, decentralized sourcing, and honest pricing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finance given priority kills work
rubrics_metrics.description: Finance is given a place ahead of work and therefore tends to kill the work and destroy the fundamental of service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not organize a business in which financiers or bankers come before doing the work. Avoid starting with largest possible capitalization and floating stock/bonds as the main purpose of a business. Prefer starting small and building from earnings. Example/antipattern: floating large corporations where promoters take the money and little goes into real foundation of the business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money-first thinking breeds fear and blocks progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Thinking first of money instead of work brings on fear of failure and this fear blocks every avenue of business—making a man afraid of competition, of changing his methods, or of doing anything which might change his condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritizing immediate profit encourages risk-aversion, opposition to innovation, and monopoly-seeking. Managers should avoid decisions driven primarily by short-term financial anxiety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service-first principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The way is clear for any one who thinks first of service—of doing the work in the best possible way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and run the business to serve the public; if you do the work well the profits and financial matters will follow. This is a foundational criterion: product/service quality should be the controlling factor in decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturer responsibility continues after sale (after-sales service)
rubrics_metrics.description: A manufacturer is not through with his customer when a sale is completed; he has then only started with his customer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide prompt repair/service and parts availability so the customer has continuous use. Example: Ford emphasized early provision of service and controlling distribution to avoid greedy local repair men. Antipattern: treating a breakdown as 'hard luck' and leaving owner to costly local repairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for the 95% (mass-market focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you discover what will give this 95 per cent. of people the best all-round service and then arrange to manufacture at the very highest quality and sell at the very lowest price, you will be meeting a demand which is so large that it may be called universal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most buyers don't know precise preferences; design a product that gives broad, all‑round service rather than many niche variants. Target the large middle market rather than extremes; this drives volume and value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardization should enable price reductions and interchangeability
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardization must not mean freezing design; it should be planning beforehand, then continually reducing price as manufacturing economies arise and making improvements interchangeable with older models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid 'standardizing' as a pretext to pick the easiest-to-make profit-maximizing design. True standardization pairs focused design with continuous manufacturing improvements whose savings are passed to customers. Aim for parts and improvements that are interchangeable so products don't become obsolete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price based on manufacturing cost and reduce with efficiencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Go to the common-sense basis of pricing on what it costs to manufacture and then reducing the cost of manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not price on what the traffic will bear. Transfer economies of scale or process improvements immediately into lower prices to build trust and market response. Example: one-price retail stores; public will trust a manufacturer who steadily reduces price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture parts where they can be made best; assemble near consumption (decentralized sourcing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern method is to have each part made where it may best be made and then assemble the parts into a complete unit at the points of consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It may be better to outsource components if quality and price are right; ownership can be scattered as long as all adopt the same service methods. Antipattern: insistence that everything be made under one roof regardless of cost/quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on financing and refinancing
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of 'refinancing' is simply the game of sending good money after bad; in the majority of cases the need of refinancing arises from bad management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refinancing postpones judgment and rewards poor management. Prefer sound operations and earnings-based growth rather than speculative financiers trying to sustain failing businesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat money as an engine of production, not a pre-charged expense
rubrics_metrics.description: Money placed in a business ceases to be money and becomes, or should become, an engine of production, and it is therefore worth what it produces—and not a fixed sum according to some scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat original investment as a fixed interest burden on operations; returns should come after the money has produced value. Antipattern: charging the business interest as if money itself had intrinsic fixed worth independent of output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace competition; do not seek monopolies through artificial means
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition is not a menace; time spent fighting competition is wasted; it had better be spent in doing the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on supplying what buyers want at the proper price rather than using patents/associations or other artifices to control price/output (example: Selden Patent association). Competing by better service and price is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous improvement and avoid inertia/habit
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a subtle danger in a man thinking that he is 'fixed' for life; habit conduces to inertia, and any disturbance affects the mind like trouble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Management must remain alert to new methods; resist complacency and evaluate processes continuously. Example: shop method studies were resisted by workmen who feared it was a ploy to increase output; overcome such resistance through trust and demonstrated benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership/work ethic: sustained personal engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: The man who has the largest capacity for work and thought is the man who is bound to succeed; a man ought to think of his business by day and dream of it by night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners/managers should remain personally engaged, continually planning improvements; accepting limited 'office hours' mentality limits potential. Tradeoffs: leisure vs horsepower—higher engagement yields greater results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principle: minimize weight and eliminate unnecessary parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess weight kills any self-propelled vehicle; strength has nothing to do with weight... Whenever any one suggests that I might increase weight or add a part, I look into decreasing weight and eliminating a part!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize light, strong, efficient design; reduce parts count and complexity. Antipattern: confusing 'weight' with 'strength' and adding unnecessary components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product attribute checklist (materials, simplicity, reliability, workmanship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasized points: good material; simplicity (ease of management); the engine; reliable ignition (redundancy); automatic oiling; simple/easy transmission (planetary type); workmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these attributes as specifications for mass-market durable goods. Ford used them in advertising and design; they contributed to reputation for toughness and simplicity. Example: Model A features and later sales growth show practical impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid planned obsolescence and excessive model proliferation
rubrics_metrics.description: Bringing out a new model each year so owners discard old ones is not service—it seeks only to provide something new, not something better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a single model refined over time with interchangeable improvements rather than yearly radically different models that force repeat purchases. Antipattern: frequent model changes designed to create repeat sales rather than add genuine customer value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing as utility: emphasize time savings and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the motor car as a utility: always ready, always sure; built to save you time and consequent money; built to take you anywhere and bring you back again on time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertise practical service benefits (time saved, punctuality, reliability, health/outdoors benefits) rather than pleasure/sporting appeals if aiming at mass, utilitarian markets.
